At the beginning of Decius's reign, when there was a persecution of the Christians, Flavianus bishop of the Romans was martyred; after him Cornelius succeeded to the bishopric for three years. Likewise Babylas, bishop of the Antiochenes, was perfected in the course of martyrdom. After him the 13th to lead Antioch was Fabius, for 3 years. Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, since many had fallen under him in the persecution of Decius, held out to them a hand of repentance to make their peace with God, and wrote about them to many of the bishops. Among these Novatus, a presbyter of the church of the Romans, lifted up by pride,

blocks: said that they must not be received, as if they had no hope of salvation left, not even if they did everything genuine that belongs to turning back; and he set himself up as leader of his own sect of those puffed up in their reasoning, who declared themselves pure. Over this a very large synod was gathered at Rome, of [sixty] bishops in number (the transcription drops the number; Eusebius, whom the chronicle copies here, has sixty) and still more presbyters and deacons, while in the other provinces too they considered separately what was to be done; and it was decreed by all that Novatus, together with those carried away with him and those who chose to agree with the man's most inhuman judgement on the brethren, should be counted as strangers to the church, but that those of the brethren who had met with the misfortune should be healed and tended with the medicines of repentance. About these things Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, wrote to Fabius, bishop of the church of the Antiochenes, telling him what the synod of the Romans had done and what those in Italy and Africa and the lands there had decided; and many others wrote much to many about the madness of Novatus and the repentance of those who had fallen in the persecution. In the 255th year from the Lord's ascension into heaven there was a persecution of the Christians, and many were martyred; among them were martyred the holy George and the holy Babylas. He was bishop of Antioch the Great, and the emperor Carinus arrived there on his way to make war on the Persians with his uncle Carus; this Carus was struck by lightning in Mesopotamia. Carinus was defeated and fled to the city of Carrhae. And the Persians besieged it closely and took him captive, and at once killed him. And they flayed him and made his skin into a sack, and having treated it with myrrh they kept it for their own glory. This Carinus died aged 35. And after his death Numerianus his brother marched against the Persians to avenge his own brother Carinus, and overcame them mightily.
Then Numerianus was slaughtered at Perinthus in Thrace, now called Heraclea, by Aper the prefect.
